extracted.intended_audience: microbiologists/taxonomists who name and describe prokaryotes; authors and publishers of taxonomic papers; journal editors; culture collection curators
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and editorial/advisory notes from the Prokaryotic Code (ICSP) governing the formation, spelling, citation, publication, and preservation of bacterial names and type material. Includes procedural requirements (when to refer to the Judicial Commission), orthography, gender, author citation conventions, publication formatting, and type strain maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perplexing names and referral to Judicial Commission (Note 2 / Rule 56a(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Perplexing names (nomina perplexa) that raise questions about status due to differing sources or confusing differences in letters may be referred to the Judicial Commission; only the Judicial Commission may place perplexing names on the list of rejected names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because decisions on names derived from different sources and differing by one or more letters affect many well-known names, the Judicial Commission alone can list such names for rejection. Example pairings given earlier (e.g., Bacillus limnophilus vs Bacillus limnophilus) illustrate perplexing names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthographic variants may be corrected by any author (Note 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orthographic variants may be corrected by any author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may correct orthographic variants without referral; see Rules 61, 62a, 62b for limits and cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to Judicial Commission for spelling doubts (Rule 58)
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is doubt about different spellings of the same name or epithet, or where two spellings are sufficiently alike to be confused, the question should be referred to the Judicial Commission, which may issue an Opinion as seems fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Judicial Commission prefers one spelling, that spelling should be used by succeeding authors. Example: the epithet 'megaterium' (over 'megatherium') in Bacillus megaterium (Opinion 1; Judicial Commission, 1951).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epithet capitalization (Rule 59)
rubrics_metrics.description: An epithet, even one derived from the name of a person, should not be written with an initial capital letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lower-case for specific epithets even when honoring persons. Example: Shigella flexneri (named after Flexner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of intentional latinizations (Rule 60)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentional latinizations involving changes in orthography of personal names, particularly those of earlier authors, must be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 're-latinize' or alter intentional latinized forms made by earlier authors. Example: Chauveau latinized as Chauvoe, so Clostridium chauvoei is derived from Chauvoe and must be preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of original spelling; correction of typographic/orthographic errors (Rule 61)
rubrics_metrics.description: The original spelling of a name or epithet must be retained, except typographic or orthographic errors. Original spelling does not refer to the use of an initial capital letter or to diacritic signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unintentional typographical or orthographic error corrected by the original author is accepted in its corrected form without affecting status/date of valid publication. Subsequent authors may also correct spellings; the abbreviation 'corrig.' may be appended but is not obligatory. Corrections do not affect the status and date of valid publication. Use this liberty with reserve, especially if the change affects the first syllable or first letter. Except for changes of gender when species are transferred (comb. nov.), no grammatical or orthographic corrections will be accepted for names on the Approved Lists, the Validation Lists and the Notification Lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthographic variants by transliteration (Rule 62a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words differing only in transliteration into Latin from other languages which do not use the Latin alphabet are to be treated as orthographic variants unless they are used as the names of taxa based upon different types, when they are to be treated as homonyms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Appendix 9 for accounts of possible orthographic variants. Example: Haemophilus and Hemophilus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's right to choose among orthographic variants (Rule 62b)
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are orthographic variants based on the same type, and there is no clear indication that one is correct, then an author has the right of choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may select which variant to use when variants are equivalent and based on the same type; consistency and clarity are advisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genitive vs adjectival personal-name epithets treated as different (Rule 63)
rubrics_metrics.description: The genitive and adjectival forms of a personal name are treated as different epithets and not as orthographic variants unless they are so similar as to cause confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For latinization of personal names see Appendix 9. Example: pasteurii (genitive noun) and pasteurianum (adjective) are different epithets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression and transcription of diacritic signs (Rule 64)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diacritic signs are not used in names or epithets in bacteriology. In names or epithets derived from words with such signs, the signs must be suppressed and the letters transcribed according to specified rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcription rules provided: (1) ä, ö, ü → ae, oe, ue; (2) é, è, ê → e; (3) ø, æ, å → oe, ae, aa, respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender of generic names (Rule 65)
rubrics_metrics.description: The gender of generic names is governed by: (1) Latin or Greek words retain classical gender of origin; authors recommended to give gender; (2) modern compounds take the gender of the last component; (3) arbitrarily formed generic names or vernacular names used as generic names take the gender assigned by their authors; if the original author failed to indicate the gender, a subsequent author has the right of choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doubtful cases should be referred to the Judicial Commission. Examples: Sarcina (Latin feminine noun). For compounds, example: Lactobacillus (masculine) from Latin lac (neuter) + bacillus (masculine). Examples of arbitrarily formed names and assigned genders are given (Desemzia, Waddlia, Afipia, Cedecea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication date and bibliographic information on publication and separates (Chapter 4A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers of periodicals and books are requested to indicate the year, month, and day of publication either on the publication itself or, in the case of a periodical, on the succeeding number. This information, as well as the title of the periodical or book from which the paper is reproduced, should also be printed on separates, tear sheets, or reprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including precise dates and source titles on reprints aids determination of priority and valid publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pagination on separates or reprints (Chapter 4A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Separates or reprints should always bear the pagination of the periodical of which they form a part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure separates show the original pagination to maintain bibliographic clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate rank and higher taxon; title should indicate new name (Chapter 4A)
rubrics_metrics.description: An author who describes and names a new taxon should indicate the rank of the taxon concerned and where possible the rank and name of the next higher taxon (e.g., family to which a new genus is allocated). The title of the work concerned should indicate that a new name is published even if the name itself is not quoted in the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear indication of rank and higher grouping in the paper and title improves discoverability and clarity. Note: Valid publication of a new name or combination requires announcement in the IJSEM (Rule 27).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to announce new name in IJSEM for valid publication (Note in Chapter 4A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Valid publication of a new name or combination requires announcement in the IJSEM (Rule 27).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should ensure compliance with Rule 27 to achieve valid publication status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and minimal standards for species descriptions and illustrations (Chapter 4A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions and illustrations of new species should be as complete as possible and conform to the minimal standards when available (see Recommendation 30b and Appendix 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Recommendation 30b and Appendix 6 for minimal required data; thorough descriptions and quality illustrations are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting scientific names in publications (Chapter 4A)
rubrics_metrics.description: For scientific names of taxa, conventions appropriate to the language of the country and to the relevant journal and publishing house should be used; these should preferably indicate scientific names by a different type face (e.g., italic) or by some other device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent typographic treatment (italics, font) helps readers identify scientific names; follow journal house style while being clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full spelling of genus at first mention (Chapter 4A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a genus should be spelled without abbreviation the first time it is used with a specific epithet in a publication and in the summary of that publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bacillus subtilis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviation of genus in series of species of same genus (Chapter 4A)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a series of species names all belonging to the same genus, it is customary to abbreviate the name of the genus in all but the first species, even if it is the first mention of the succeeding species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bacillus subtilis, B. polymyxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard abbreviation for later use of genus (Chapter 4A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Later use of the name of the species previously cited usually has the name of the genus abbreviated, commonly to the first letter of the generic name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: B. subtilis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous abbreviations when genus initials clash (Chapter 4A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If species are listed belonging to two or more genera which have the same initial letter, the generic name should be used in full.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a single-letter abbreviation when multiple genera share the same initial; write out the genus to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing multiple authors (et al.) (Chapter 4B(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: When the new name of a taxon is published under two authors, both are cited; when there are more than two authors and no definite designation of a single individual as the author of the name, the citation may be made by listing the names of all the authors or by giving the name of the first author, followed by the abbreviation 'et al.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full author list for two authors; for >2, either list all or use 'FirstAuthor et al.' depending on context and space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation format when name published in another's work ('in') (Chapter 4B(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new name or combination by one author is published in a work of another author, the word 'in' should be used in the literature cited to connect the names of the two authors. The name of the author of the name of the taxon precedes the name of the author in whose work it is contained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example format: Streptomyces reticuli Waksman, S. A., and A. T. Henrici in Breed, R. S., et al., [citation].

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicating synonymy with 'pro synon.' (Chapter 4B(3)(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing a name published as a synonym, the words 'as synonym' or 'pro synon.' should be added to the citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to indicate that the cited name was published as a synonym (see Rule 24a for types of synonym). Example: Pseudomonas pyocyanea pro synon. Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'ex' for names published from another's manuscript (Chapter 4B(3)(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author publishes a name from a manuscript of another author, or revives another author's name, whether as a synonym or not, the word 'ex' should be used to connect the names of the two authors. The name of the author who publishes the name precedes that of the original author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Achromobacter xylosoxidans (ex Yabuuchi and Ohyama 1971) Yabuuchi and Yano 1981 nom. rev. A subsequent author would cite the revived name accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'non' to indicate earlier homonym (Chapter 4B(3)(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing in synonymy a name invalidated by an earlier homonym, the citation should be followed by the name of the author of the earlier homonym preceded by the word 'non', preferably with the date of publication added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Achromobacter Yabuuchi and Yano 1981 (non 'Achromobacter' Bergey et al. 1923).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing original spelling with 'sic' when alterations adopted (Chapter 4B(3)(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a name or epithet is adopted with alterations from the form as originally published, including the use of a corrected spelling, the original spelling should be cited in any list of synonyms of the corrected name. The original spelling is followed by the term 'sic' in parentheses to indicate that the original spelling is accurately cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bacillus pantothenticus (sic). This preserves citation of the original form in synonym lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicating nomen nudum with 'nom. nud.' (Chapter 4B(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: In the citation of a bare name (nomen nudum), the status of the name should be indicated by adding 'nom. nud.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bare name (nomen nudum) means a name published without a description or a reference to a previously published description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicating conserved names with 'nom. cons.' (Chapter 4B(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: A conserved name (nomen conservandum) shall be indicated by the addition of the abbreviation 'nom. cons.' to the citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Pseudomonas Migula 1894 nom. cons. (Opinion 5). Use this to show formal conservation of a name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and deposition of type material; include record in publication (Chapter 4C)
rubrics_metrics.description: The utmost importance should be given to the preservation of the original 'type' material on which the description of a new species or subspecies is based. Preserved and living specimens should be maintained in a bacteriological laboratory, more particularly in one of the permanently established culture collections, and a record of this fact should be included in the publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Rules 18a, 27 and 30. State in the publication where the type material is deposited (culture collection accession numbers, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable maintenance methods for type material (Chapter 4C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance may be by a variety of methods, e.g., in a medium, in a host by passage, in cells or exudates, or in the frozen or dried state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select appropriate preservation methods for organism physiology and long-term stability; indicate method in records/publication when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize change in type strains; avoid repeated subculture (Chapter 4C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every precaution should be taken to maintain such cultures with a minimum amount of change. Repeated subculture may lead to phenotypic or genotypic changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit passages and use preservation approaches (cryopreservation, lyophilization) that minimize genetic/phenotypic drift; document strain history.
